LAW MINISTERS' MEETING 1995
HYDERABAD RESOLUTION
           
The plenary meeting of Law Secretaries and Law Ministers was held in Hyderabad during 23-25 November,
1995 to consider the following items:
 
I.                    Implementation of -
(i)                  Resolution adopted by the Chief Ministers and Chief Justice (1993);
(ii)                Calcutta Resolution of Law Ministers (1994);
II.                 Alternative Dispute Resolution;
III.               Reforms in Legal Education and Entry into Legal Profession.
 
2.
                  The Law Secretaries met under the chairmanship of Dr. P.C. Rao, Union Law Secretary, on 23 November,
1995.  The Law Secretaries recommended a draft Resolution on the items referred to above for consideration of the Law
Ministers.
 
3.
                  The Law Ministers met under the Chairmanship of Shri H.R. Bhardwaj, Union Minister of State for Law, Justice
and Company Affairs, on 25 November 1995 to consider the aforesaid draft Resolution.
 
4.         The Chief Justice of India, Shri Justice A.M. Ahmadi, the Chief Minister of Andhra Pradesh,  Shri N.
Chandrababu Naidu, Shri Justice K. jayachandra reddy, Chairman, law Commission of India and Shri P.S. Mishra, Chief
justice of Andhra Pradesh High Court delivered special addresses at the meeting.
 
5.         The Law Ministers expressed their appreciation on the work done in the Working Group of Law Secretaries and
of Law Ministers which met in Bhubaneswar from 22 to 24 September 1995 as also in the Plenary Meeting of Law
Secretaries which met in Hyderabad on 23 November 1995.
 
I           Implementation of-(i) Resolution adopted by the Chief Ministers and Chief Justice (1993); and (ii)
Calcutta Resolution of Law Ministers (1994).
 
6.         The Law Ministers took note of Doc.No. LMM/IMP/1/95 containing the statement showing follow up action
taken on the recommendations made by the Chief Ministers and the Chief Justices in their 1993 Resolution as also by the
Law Ministers in their 1994 Calcutta  Resolution.
 
7.         The Law Ministers expressed their satisfaction that the Legal Services Authorities Act, 1987 had been brought
into force.  They noted, however, that only the State Governments of Sikkim, Himachal Pradesh and Rajasthan had taken
steps to enforce the Act in their jurisdictions and called upon the State Government to taken steps immediately for the
purposed of bringing the said Act into force in their respective jurisdictions.
 
8.         The Law Ministers were happy to note that, in keeping with the recommendations of the Chief Ministers and
Chief Justices in their New Delhi Resolution, the Government of India, in consultation with the Chief Justice of India
and the Chief Justice of High Courts, had reviewed the Judge-strength in the High Courts and increased the number of
Judges in the High Courts of Madras, Kerala, Karnataka and Gujarat.  They further noted with appreciation that the
Government of India, issued guidelines recommending that action for appointment of  a High Court Judge should be
initiated at least four months in advance of the occurrence of a vacancy.  The Law Ministers expressed the hope that

SUB-COMMITTEE
file:///D/Committee%20on%20Home%20Affairs/85threport%20.htm[30-06-2016 17:49:13]
these guidelines would be strictly observed by all the constitutional functionaries.  They recalled the recommendation of
Chief Ministers and Chief Justices that the number of vacancies in each High Court to be filled up from the judicial
officers of subordinate judiciary might go upto 40% and noted that the 40% limit was a accepted by the High Courts.
 
9.         The Law Ministers noted that, in consonance with the recommendations made by them in their Calcutta
Resolution, the Government of India had invited the Law Commission of India to undertake a comprehensive  revision
of the Indian Penal Code, 1860, the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973 and the Evidence Act, 1872.
 
10.       The Law Ministers noted with appreciation that the Government of Rajasthan decided to establish courts at the
Tehsil level to assist rural litigation and asked the other State Governments to initiate similar steps with a view to
providing inexpensive and speedy resolution of rural litigation.
 
11.       The Law Ministers, while noting that some Sate Governments had taken steps to furnish courts with modern
equipment, underlined the need to expedite the process of computerising the records and judgments of courts.  They
noted with special satisfaction  that the High Court of Gujarat had been fully computerised and that the Government of
Gujarat had commenced the task of computerising the district courts and city civil courts in a phased manner.  They
expressed the hope that the other State Governments would also take similar steps on priority basis so as to enable the
courts to deal with the problem of arrears of cases as expeditiously as possible.
 
12.       The Law Ministers recalled the earlier recommendation of the Chief Ministers and Chief Justices that the
provisions of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973 in regard to the appointment of Judicial Magistrates of the Second
Class, Special Judicial Magistrates and Special Metropolitan Magistrates should be put to use by identifying cases which
they would be empowered to deal with under the Code.  While the State Governments of Assam, Andhra Pradesh and
Himachal Pradesh had taken steps in this regard, the other State Governments had not reported much progress in this
regard.  The Law Ministers noted that the Supreme Court of India had issued directions with a view to ensure that the
machinery contemplated by sections 6(4), 13, 18, 260 and 261 of the Code of Criminal Procedure be put into effect for
clearing the backlog of petty criminal cases [vide kadra Pahadiya Vs. State of Bihar, 1995 (6) SCALE 121].  The Law
Ministers underlined the need to take immediate action as recommended by the Chief Ministers and Chief Justices in this
regard as also directed by the Supreme Court of India.
 
13.       The Law Ministers recalled that the Chief Ministers and Chief Justices had earlier recommended the need for
evolving appropriate guidelines for preventing indiscriminate strikes by lawyers.  They noted that the Supreme Court of
India, by its order dated 7 December 1994, directed the following interim measures in the matter of lawyers' strikes:
 
"(i)        In the rare instance where any association of lawyers (including statutory Bar Councils) considers it
imperative to call upon and/or advise members of the legal profession to abetain from appearing in courts on any
occasion, it must be left open to any individual member/members of that association to be free to appear without
let, fear or hindrance or any other coercive step.
 
(ii)        No such member who appears in courts or otherwise practices his legal profession, shall be visited with
any adverse or penal consequences, whatever, by any association of lawyers, any shall not suffer any expulsion
or threat of expulsion therefrom.
 
(iii)       The above will not preclude other forms of protest by practicing lawyers in courts such as, for instance,
wearing of arm bands and other forms of protest which in no way interrupt or disrupt the court proceedings or
adversely affect  the interest of the litigant.  Any such form of protest shall not however be derogatory to the
court or to the profession.
 
(iv)       Office bearers of a Bar Association (including bar Councils) responsible for taking decisions mentioned

SUB-COMMITTEE
file:///D/Committee%20on%20Home%20Affairs/85threport%20.htm[30-06-2016 17:49:13]
in clause (1) above shall ensure that such decisions are implemented in the spirit of what is stated in clauses (1),
(2) and (3) above."
 
            The Law Ministers further noted that the aforesaid order had been circulated by the Bar Council of India to the
State Bar Councils and Bar Associations for necessary action and expressed the hope that all concerned would abide by
the Court's  order in its letter and spirit and extend full cooperation to the courts in this regard.
 
14.       The Law Ministers, while noting that some progress was made in the matter of implementation of the earlier
recommendations made by them as also by the Chief Ministers and Chief Justices, observed that a number of
recommendations still remained to be implemented.  They declared that any delay or inaction in this regard would not
only make the recommendations weak but also render their collective endeavours a wasted effort.  The Law Ministers
noted that the country was passing through a critical moment in the matter of administration of justice on account of the
backlog of cases in courts and expressed their determination to pursue with vigour the recommendations made by them.
 
15.       The Law Ministers further expressed their dissatisfaction that about 16 State Governments could not fully utilize
the  amount released by the Central Government based on a formula provided by the Planning Commission of India. 
They called upon all concerned to give attention that was due to the working of courts which played an important part in
the maintenance of rule of law and in the achievement of the objective of building a welfare State and equitable social
order.
 
II.
                 Alternative Dispute Resolution
 
16.       The Law Ministers recalled that the Chief Ministers and the Chief Justices, in their Resolution adopted on 4
December 1993, declared that courts were not in a position to bear the entire burden of justice system, that a number of
disputes lent themselves to resolution by alternative modes such as arbitration, mediation and negotiation and that the
disputants should take advantage of alternative dispute resolution (ADR) which previded procedural flexibility, saved
valuable time and money and avoided the stress of a conventional trial.
 
17.       The Law Ministers further recalled that, in their Resolution adopted at Calcutta on 17 November 1994, they
recommended that a comprehensive law on arbitration and conciliation be enacted based largely on UNCITRAL, Model
Law on International Commercial Arbitration and UNCITRAL Conciliation Rules covering both international and
domestic arbitration and conciliation.  The Law Ministers noted with satisfaction that was introduced in Parliament in
consonance with the recommendation made in the Calcutta Resolution.  The Law Ministers hoped that the Bill would be
enacted as early as possible.  They considered that the proposed law on arbitration and conciliation would greatly
strengthen settlement of disputes by ADR.
 
18.       The Law Ministers were of the view that ADR should be the preferred method for settlement of a wide range of
disputes, especially commercial and other civil disputes.  They underlined the urgent need to establish infrastructure
facilities for strengthening ADR movement in India.  In this connection they noted with satisfaction, the establishment of
the International Centre for Alternative Dispute Resolution (ICADR)  in New Delhi which was inaugurated by the Prime
Minister of India on 6 October 1995.  They recommended that ADR mechanism should be established throughout the
country.  The Law Ministers recommended that, among others, the Central Government, the State Governments, public
sector undertakings and chambers of commerce and industry should render such financial and other assistance as they
could in promoting ADR organisations in India.  They further recommended that training courses should be organised
for ADR  neutrals so as to equip them with a reasonable standard of expertise and skill.
 
19.       The Law Ministers emphasised the desirability of courts developing ADR schemes as an integral part of the court
system.  They called upon the Central Government, State Governments and the various public sector undertakings to
incorporate ADR clauses in their contracts.

SUB-COMMITTEE
file:///D/Committee%20on%20Home%20Affairs/85threport%20.htm[30-06-2016 17:49:13]
 
20.       The Law Minis6ters also noted that the legal education in India  trained law students only in court systems
involving adversarial proceedings.  They felt that legal education should be so oriented as to train law students in
innovative approaches to dispute-resolution.  They called upon the Bar Council of India, the University Grants
Commission and the Universities to revise the syllabi for legal education with a view to incorporating therein specific
courses on ADR processes which are designed to develop dispute-settlement skills of law students and to prepare them
as problem solvers.
 
III        Reforms in Legal Education and Entry into Legal Profession
 
21.       The Law Ministers considered the recommendations made by the Law Commission of India in its 14
th Report,
the Committee of Judges, consisting of Hon'ble Shri Justice A.M. Ahmadi (as he then was), Hon'ble Shri Justice M.
Jagannatha Rao,  the Chief Justice of Delhi High Court and Hon'ble Shri Justice B.N. Kirpal, the Chief Justice of Gujarat
High Court (as he then was), in its report of 17 October 1994,  the Committee on Subordinate Legislation (Tenth Lok
Saber) in its 15 th Report presented on 16 December 1994 and the University Grants Commission's Reconstituted Panel
on Law in its report submitted on 27  th  December 1994.  The law Ministers took note of the Working Paper on the
agenda item presented by the conference secretariat of the Ministry of Law, Justice and Company Affairs
[No.LMM/(LE)/1/95] and the Bhubaneswar Statement of Law Ministers' Working Group on Legal Education
[No.LMM/(LE)/2/95].
 
22.       The Law Ministers expressed their concern at the deteriorating standards in legal education.  They observed that
the Supreme Court of India had also recently drawn attention to the fall in the standard of legal education.  They were of
the opinion that there was an urgent need for reforms in legal education.  The Law Ministers also noted that the quality
of the legal services and administration of justice depended largely on the standard of legal education.
 
23.       The Law Ministers generally welcomed the recommendations made by the bodies referred to above.  They
considered that the fall in the standard of legal education was not on account of any deficiencies in the legal framework, 
but primarily on account of week enforcement of the legal provisions by the competent bodies.  They were of the
opinion that a successful strategy for improving legal education ought to take into account the following elements,
among others:
 
(i)         The Bar Council of India, the body entrusted with the task of maintaining the standard of legal education,
should play a more effective role in discharging its functions under the provisions of the Advocates Act.
 
(ii)        There should be an adequate number of law colleges with proper infrastructure including experienced
law teachers and staff so that sufficient number of well trained and properly equipped law graduates in all
branches of law would be available to meet the growing demands of the society.
 
(iii)       Professional legal education should be a five-year system of law course 10-plus-2 level.  However,
students who were undergoing three year law course should be eligible to enrol as advocates till an
appropriate amendment  was made to the Advocates Act, 1961 prescribing a five-year system of law
course.
 
(iv)       Legal education, which prepares students for the practice of  law, should be allowed  only through whole-
time law colleges or University Department.
 
(vi)
              In addition to a 5-year system of law course after 10-plus-2 level, it should be open to a university to
offer a 3-year law course after 10-plus-2 level for the benefit of people who wanted to gain knowledge of

SUB-COMMITTEE
file:///D/Committee%20on%20Home%20Affairs/85threport%20.htm[30-06-2016 17:49:13]
law and advance their careers in areas other than legal profession.
 
(vii)             It should be strictly ensured that only such law colleges were allowed to come into existence, whose
infrastructure facilities wee in conformity with  the standards prescribed by or under the Advocates Act,
1961 and the rules made thereunder.  The practice of granting temporary approval to law colleges should
be discontinued forthwith.  Existing law colleges offering 3-year law course should not be allowed to
switch over to 5-year law course, unless they satisfied the prescribed standards for offering such course
and also obtained prior approval of the Bar Council of India.  Greater vigilance was called for in the
matter of extending approval to law colleges or continuing such approval to colleges which did not
maintain prescribed standards.
 
(viii)
           It would be appropriate if the bar Council of India obtained the comments of the concerned State
Government also in the matter of affiliation/disaffiliation of law colleges, especially having regard to the
fact that State Governments maintained several law colleges.
 
(ix)              A law college which failed to satisfy at any time the prescribed standards should be given a specific
time-limit within which it could take remedial measures and, if it failed to take such measures within such
time-limit, action should be taken to withdraw the approval extended to such college.  The Bar council or
India should consider using the services of the national Assessment and Accreditation Council (NAAC),
set up by the University Grants Commission, to evaluate law colleges at prescribed intervals in term of
the norms laid down by the Bar Council of India.  Such an independent, scientific assessment would help
the Bar Council of India to proceed against the erring institutions according to law.
 
(x)
                There should also be a National Law School type of college in each State so that it could serve as a
model institution for other law colleges in that State.
 
(xi)              The Legal Education Committee of the Bar Council of India should establish criteria for determining as
to how many colleges could be allowed to operate in a given area, having regard to such factors as the
size of the area, size of the population in the area, need for lawyers in that area, the number of law
colleges and courts in the neighbouring areas, etc., so as to avoid undue concentration of law colleges in a
given area.
 
(xii)
             With a view to securing strict enforcement of the relevant provisions of the Advocates Act and the rules
made thereunder, the Legal Education Committee of the Bar Council of India should consist of, among
others, representatives of the judiciary, Union Ministry of law, Justice and Company Affairs, University
Grants Commission, established law colleges/law faculties and institutions specialising in legal  research. 
The recommendation of such a body should, as a general rule,  be accepted by the Bar Council of India. 
The recommendations of the Legal Education Committee should in no event be rejected unless such
rejection was supported by a majority of the total membership of the Council and by a majority of two-
thirds of the members of the Council present and voting.
 
(xiii)
           Admission into law colleges should be through a common entrance examination, held either at the
national level or at the Sate level, and entry into the colleges should be made conditional upon a candidate
securing a minimum of 50% marks in such examination.  Eligibility for appearing in the entrance
examination should also be made conditional upon a candidate securing a minimum of 50% marks in the
qualifying examination.
 
(xiv)
           It should be made mandatory that, in addition to the lecture method, the law colleges would invariably
provide for the case method, tutorials, problem method, moot courts, mock trails, etc., in imparting legal
education and that marks were awarded on the basis of participation of students in these activities.  A

SUB-COMMITTEE
file:///D/Committee%20on%20Home%20Affairs/85threport%20.htm[30-06-2016 17:49:13]
Minimum of 75% attendance should be insisted upon in such activities.
 
(xv)            Law examinations should increasingly be problem-based to enable students to develop skills of analysis
of facts and reasoning essential for the profession.
 
(xvi)           Post-graduate courses in law should not be allowed to be taught either in morning/evening colleges or
through correspondence courses.  Such courses should not be allowed in institutions which did not have
libraries that possessed latest books and periodicals in law and competent teachers and staff.
 
(xvii)         Management of every law college should include judges, experienced legal practitioners, law teacher
and academics.
 
(xviii)        Practical training should be given its due place in professional legal education.  The present scheme as
prescribed by the Bar Council of India Rules should be continued by colleges teaching law.  However,
this alone would not be adequate to give the new entrant to the Bar the necessary professional skills and
standard of ethics.  For this, a scheme of one year's apprenticeship under a Senior Advocate or an
advocate with atlest 15 years of practice followed by an examination on procedural subjects organised on
a six-monthly basis by State Bar Council must be introduced with immediate effect.
 
(xix)           The Bar Council of India, research institutions in the field of law and other bodies dealing with areas of
interest to lawyers should be invited to organise refresher courses for practising lawyers which benefited
them in the pursuit of their legal profession.
 
(xx)
            Law colleges imparting legal education for admission to practice should be encouraged to extend
supportive services to the legal aid apparatue.  This would enable the students not only to extend technical
services to the community they live in, but also to learn a variety of professional skills related to court
procedures and alternative dispute resolution systems.  Legal Aid Committees should also be encouraged
to develop linkages with professional law colleges in respect of matters falling within their jurisdiction.
 
(xxi)
           In view of the increased responsibilities of the Bar Councils for maintaining standards in the profession,
and having regard to the inadequate income of the Bar Councils, a higher enrolment fee not exceeding
Rs.2000/-should be prescribed, leaving it to the Bar Council of India and the State Bar Councils to
prescribe from time to time a reasonable fee within that limit fix a reasonable  amount not exceeding
Rs.500/- towards renewal of certificate of enrolment.
 
24.       The Law Ministers noted with satisfaction that the Bar Council of India and the University Grants Commission
were in general agreement with the aforesaid recommendations in the matter of reforms in legal education and entry into
legal profession.  The Law Ministers further noted with appreciation that the Bar Council of India had resolved to
introduce one-year pre-enrolment training for law graduates seeking to enter the legal profession.
 
25.       The Law Ministers were of the opinion that the Advocates Act, 1961, and the rules made thereunder be amended
immediately for giving effect to the above recommendations.
 
26.       The Law Ministers expressed their deep appreciation to the Government of Andhra Pradesh for inviting them to
hold the present plenary meeting in Hyderabad and making all efforts for its successful completion.

III.       CASE MANAGEMENT AND STATUTORY TIME LIMIT FOR DISPOSAL OF CASES
 
STEPS TAKEN FOR REDUCING PENDENCY
 
            Briefly stated, various measures that have been taken by the Government include amendment of the Civil
Procedure Code and Criminal Procedure Code, increase in the number of posts of Judges/Judicial Officers, appointment
of Special Judicial/Metropolitan Magistrates and adoption of other alternative modes of dispute resolution including
organising  Lok Adalats.  In addition, the Supreme Court and High Courts have taken a number of steps for expeditious
disposal of cases, viz; grouping and classification of cases involving similar question of law, setting up specialised
benches, computerization of listing of cases, etc.
 
COMPUTERISATION IN COURTS

SUB-COMMITTEE
file:///D/Committee%20on%20Home%20Affairs/85threport%20.htm[30-06-2016 17:49:13]
 
            The Supreme Court of India, 18High Courts and 430 District Courts have been computerised as per information
made available by the national Information Centre (NIC).  Under the Centrally Sponsored Scheme for the development
of infrastructural  facilities for the judiciary, an amount of Rs. 208.28 lakhs has been released by the Government during
the year 2000-2001 to various States/UTs for the use of computers in courts.
 
            The Supreme Court and all High Courts have been interconnected through NICNET.  Daily cause lists are being
generated through computer.  Important reported cases of the Supreme Court are available on NICNET.  Facilitation
centres/enquiry counters have been established in the Supreme Court, and the High Courts of Gujarat, Madhya Pradesh,
Calcutta and Andhra Pradesh.  Other High Courts have been requested to set up facilitation centres/enquiry counters.
 
            In addition to above steps for implementing other judicial reforms have also been undertaken by the Government.
 
PROPOSED AMENDMENTS IN CRIMINAL PROCEDURE CODE
 
The Law Commission of India in its 154
th Report has made a number of recommendations for speedy disposal of
criminal cases.  The Law Commission in its Report has not recommended fixing of time limit for criminal and other
cases which are pending in the lower courts, except to prevent delay in trials in rape cases including child rape cases. 
The following proviso was recommended to be inserted to prescribe a time limit of two months from the date of the
commencement of examination of witnesses for completion of trial:
 
"Provided that when the inquiry or trial related to an offence under section 376 to 376 (E) of the Indian
Penal Code, judgement shall, as far as possible, be delivered within a period of two months from the date
of commencement of the examination of witnesses."
 
AMENDMENT IN THE CIVIL PROCEDURE CODE
 
            The Civil Procedure Code (Amendment) Act, 1999, as assented to by the President, will prove useful in the field
of speedy disposal of cases by the Indian Judicial System.  The proposed Amendment Act, 1999 inter alia provides fixed
time frames at various stages of civil proceedings such as filing of written statements, service of summons, framing of
issues, restriction on grant of number of adjournments etc.
 
DIRECTIONS OF THE CHIEF JUSTICE OF INDIA FOR SPEEDY DISPOSAL OF CASES
 
            The Hon'ble Chief Justice of India has also written to various High Courts to dispose of all cases which are
pending for more than seven years in various courts.
 
SETTING UP OF 1734 ADDITIONAL COURTS UNDER THE SPECIAL PROBLEMS GRANT PROVIDED BY
THE XITH FINANCE COMMISSION
 
On       the initiative taken by the Department of Justice, the Eleventh Finance Commission has provided a special
problems grant of Rs.502.90 crore for disposing of about 2 million pending cases in the country by creation of 1734
additional courts @ 5 courts per district in the country for the period 2001-2005.

6.         The Income Tax Appellate Tribunal, constituted under the Income Tax Act, 1961 deals with second appeals in
all matters relating to direct taxes, and appeals against orders of revision of Commissioners as well as orders of
acquisition of properties under Chapter XXA of the Income Tax Act, 1961. 
 
6.1       The Tribunal is headed by a President, who is  assisted by one Senior Vice-President and seven Vice-Presidents. 
The present strength of Members of Tribunal is 106 for 53 Benches spread over 25 cities.  There are normally two
Members in a Bench known as Judicial Member and Accountant Member having substantial experience in their
respective fields.
 
6.2       The matters which the Appellate Tribunal disposes of are of vital importance involving revenue to the tune of
millions of rupees. The Tribunal is entrusted with the task of deciding intricate questions of law and facts.  The presence
of both the Judicial and Accountant Members ensure that questions of facts which arise for their consideration are
properly enquired into and that the accountancy points, as also the legal angle, have been weighed properly.
 
6.3    The pendency of appeals with ITAT has had  been a matter of serious concern for  the Committee. It has been
urging upon the Government to reduce the huge pendency of cases. The Committee in its 45
th  ( 1998) and 61st Reports
( 2000) had expressed its displeasure over the delay in making all the additional Benches (To reduce the pendency a
decision was taken by the Government to create 15 additional Benches, of the Tribunal in addition to the 38 existing
Benches with effect from 1
st April, 1997.) functional which had a direct bearing on the unrelenting  pendency.
 
6.4       In its 72
nd  Report ( 2001) on the Demands for Grants ( 2001-02) of Ministry of Law, Justice and Company
Affairs,  the Committee had observed that the pendency was still very high as the average pendency per Bench was
about 5000 appeals.  The Committee also recommended to the Government to initiate all necessary measures  and see to
it that pendency was  reduced substantially.
 
6.5   The Secretary informed the Committee that ITAT has a pendency of approximately 2,07,000 cases as on March 1,
2002 as against 2,44,320 in the corresponding month during the previous year. He further elaborated that all the
additional benches have since been made functional and due to various efforts made to reduce pendency of cases, the
pendency which had once crossed the mark of three lakh has now come down to 2,07,000 clearly indicating an arrest of
the increase in pendency.
 
6.6 The Committee notes the state of pendency of appeals which has  gone down from about 5000  pending cases per
bench in March 2001 to about 4000 pending cases per bench at the end of February, 2002. However, it feels it is still
very high by any standard and the Government should continue it efforts in the right direction and hopes that the
pendency would come down substantially by the end of the current financial year.

representation of SCs, STs and OBCs in the appointment of Notaries, as the ‘Memorial’, the basic document for

National Legal Services Authority (NALSA)
           
9.      The National Legal Services Authority (NALSA), a statutory body constituted under the National Legal Services
Authorities Act, 1987, as amended by the Act of 1994, is responsible for providing free legal assistance to poor and
weaker sections of the society on the basis of equal opportunity. NALSA is engaged in providing legal services, legal
aid and speedy justice through Lok Adalats.  The Authority has its office at New Delhi and is headed by the Chief
Justice of India who is the ex-officio Patron-in-Chief.  Similarly, State Legal Services Authorities have been constituted
in every State Capital.  Supreme Court Legal Services Committee, High Court Legal Services Committees, District
Legal Services Authorities and Taluk Legal Services Committees have also been constituted in every State.
 
9.1   During  2001 about 4.16 lakh persons had benefited through court-oriented legal aid programmes . Of them, about
86,650 persons belonged to the Scheduled Castes, about 14,850 to the Scheduled Tribes, more than 60,900 were women
and about 14,600 were children. It  was expected that legal aid would  be dispensed to more than  2.10 lakh persons
during the last four months of the financial year, i.e. from December 2001 to March 2002.
 
9.2   About 2025 Lok Adalats had been organised during 2001, wherein more than 6.93 lakh cases had been settled.  In
about 40,650 Motor Vehicles Accident Claims Cases compensation amounting to over Rs.221 crore had been awarded. 
Other categories of cases, such as, Land Acquisition, Petty Criminal, Civil and Matrimonial had also been settled in
these Lok Adalats.
 
9.3  A nationwide publicity campaign was launched on 9
th November, 2001 to create mass awareness with publication
relating to availability of free legal services under the Legal Services Authorities Act.
 
9.4   The  Secretary in his deposition before the Committee said that as per information available with NALSA, as on 31
December 2001 about 40.40 lakh persons have benefited through court-oriented legal aid programmes. He further said
till date about 1,24,000 Lok Adalats have been organised  since its  inception,  wherein about 1 crore 36 lakh cases have
been settled.
 
9.5   To a query of the Committee as to what was the response of the Department of Expenditure to the letter dated
10.10.2001 of the Law Secretary regarding finalisation of the accounting procedure of the National Legal Aid Fund so
that the fund could be operationalised, the Ministry informed the Committee that a meeting was held under the
Chairmanship of Additional Secretary, Department of Expenditure on 16 November 2001 to discuss the issue.  It was
also attended by representatives from Controller of Accounts, Department of Economic Affairs and C & A.G.  It was
decided that the common format of accounts already made applicable to the Central autonomous organisations in
consultation with the C &AG would be adopted by the legal services authorities at the national, state and district levels
for the accounting procedure of the National Legal Aid Fund.
 
9.6  The Ministry further informed the Committee that a draft Notification notifying the adoption of common
accounting format for the Fund has been prepared after obtaining the concurrence of the Chief Controller of Accounts
regarding the manner of administration of the Fund and sent to  NALSA for their concurrence.
 
9.7  A point was raised in the Committee that Lok Adalats and the Legal Services Authorities at various levels are
functioning without  permanent buildings  and with very poor infrastructural facilities.
 
 9.8  The Committee urges upon  the Government to operationalise  the accounting procedure of the National Legal Aid
Fund without further delay .  It  is also of the view that the Fund
should be utilised judiciously  so that,  needy people receive  legal aid. Further the Committee recommends to the
Government to provide funds for construction of  buildings for the Lok Adalats and the Legal Services Authorities at

19.       The Election Commission is entrusted by the Constitution to play the role of superintendence, direction and
control of elections.   However,  Legislative Department is accountable to the Parliament so far as the functioning of
Election Commission is concerned.  Besides the entire electoral process  in the country, the Election Commission has

the use of electronic voting machines in all the Parliamentary and Assembly constituencies in the country.  
 
Electors Photo Identity Cards
 
20.  According to Annual Report of Ministry of Law, Justice & Company Affairs  2001-2002, as on 26.2.2002 , 64.25
percent of electors have been provided with photo identity cards in the country.  The States like West Bengal and Kerala
have equipped more than 80% of their voters with the photo identity cards.  However, States like Bihar (and Jharkhand)
have been able to give photo identity cards to only 37.10 percent  of their voters.

20.1  The Committee wanted to know the reasons of such a state of affairs in Bihar and Jhakhand as far as distribution
of photo identity cards was concerned and also whether  the Election Commission had  drawn  up  any time schedule  to
complete the work in the country and how much money had already been spent on this Scheme.
 
20.2  The Department on behalf of  the Election Commission of India  informed that  the programme relating to the
Electors’ Photo Identity Cards (EPIC) started in undivided Bihar during the year 1994 and continued till 1997.  The
Government of undivided Bihar seemed to have been confronted with various problems in implementing the EPIC
programme, such as contractual problems, paucity of funds and administrative problems which resulted in slow
progress.  Three General Elections viz. two to Lok Sabha in 1998 and 1999 and another to the State Legislative
Assembly in 2000 were held and since the entire attention was diverted to the conduct of these elections, the work of
computerisation of rolls and preparation of the photo identity cards could not be taken up.  It was also  pointed out that
the officers of the Bihar Government were on strike in August-September 2000 and because of this, the revision of
electoral rolls w.e.f. 1.1.2002 and preparation of photo identity cards could not be taken up.  In addition, the new State
of Jharkhand was created in 2000 by bifurcating the State of Bihar.  It was also  stated  that in May, 2000, the Election
Commission had issued revised and detailed guidelines for the preparation of the photo identity cards.  According to
these guidelines, the computerisation of the electoral rolls is a pre-requisite for the preparation of the photo identity
cards.  The Committee was informed that attempts are under way to computerise the rolls district-wise so that the
programme of photo identity cards could be restarted in the State.
 
20.3   The Department further informed that   the scheme of issue of photo identity cards to electors is not a project but a
programme for the completion of which no time limit can be fixed as the registration of electors is a continuous and
ongoing process (excepting for a brief period between the last date for filing nomination and completion of electoral
process) on account of more number of persons becoming eligible for the right of franchise on attaining the age of 18
years as also due to the movement of electors.
 
20.4  The Department also informed that a sum of Rs. 429,45,61,710/- has so far been released by the Central
Government to the States/Union Territories towards reimbursement of its share of expenditure on the scheme of
Electors’ Photo Identity Cards.
 
20.5  The Committee takes a serious view of the tardy progress of   issue of  Electors’ Photo Identity Cards   to voters in
Bihar and Jharkhand and finds the explanation  given by the Government for not having any time limit for completion
of the programme of  issuing of photo identity cards to all the voters in the country, unacceptable. The Committee also
does not agree with the Ministry that issuing the photo identity cards is a programme  and not a  project and feels that 
this definitional escape reflects lack  of seriousness in completing the project in a given time frame.  Therefore, the
Committee urges the Government to take up the matter with the Election Commission so that Electors’ Photo Identity
Card are issued to all the electors in the country within a fixed time schedule.

Delinking of Budget of Department of Justice
 
24.       The Committee has been persistently recommending to set right the anomaly relating to the budget presentation
and administrative control over Department of Justice since 1995 through its 17
th Report (1995), 31st and 34th Reports
(1996), 39th Report (1997), 45th Report (1998), 56th Report (1999), 61st Report (2000), 69 th  and 72 nd Reports ( 2001)
to either make it an independent Department or merge the budget with the Ministry of Home Affairs. As per the present
scheme the Demands for Grants of the Department of Justice is met from that of the Ministry of Law, Justice and
Company Affairs whereas the Department is under the administrative control of the Ministry of Home Affairs. 
 
24.1     In the earlier replies the Ministry had reasoned that if the Demands for Grants for the Department of Justice were
transferred to the Ministry of Home Affairs, the Demands will be presented to the Parliament by the Minister of Home
Affairs and the Ministerial responsibility for the Department of Justice will, perhaps, shift from the Minister for Law
and Justice to the Minister of Home Affairs. Such a consequence would be neither in tune with the recommendation of
the Law Commission nor with those of the Administrative Reforms Commission. Such a course would also not be
consistent with the decision taken in 1971 while creating a new Department of Justice when it was decided to continue
the administrative association of the Department of Justice with the Home Secretary as the Secretary, Justice, while
keeping the Minister level responsibility for the Department of Justice with the Minister for Law, Justice and Company
Affairs.
 
24.2   The Department in its Action Taken Note on the recommendations of the Committee on Home Affairs contained
in its 72
nd Report on Demands for Grants ( 2001-02) has said that after due consideration, advice of the Cabinet
Secretariat had been sought on the course of action to be adopted in this regard and the Department would take a final
view after receiving their advice.
 
24.3   The Department has now communicated the observation of the Cabinet Secretariat to the Committee which is as
follows:
 
“ The mere fact that the Home Secretary holds additional charge of the Department of Justice, does not affect the

status or entity of the Department as an independent full-fledged Department.
 
The fact that the Demands for Grants for the Department are made separately, and not linked to the Home
Ministry, is actually a recognition of the status of the Department of Justice as a separate Department. This
position can be further confirmed/ resolved with the Ministry of Finance.
 
In view of the above, as per the Government of India ( Allocation of Business) Rules, 1961, the Department of
Justice is a full fledged separate Department, headed by Secretary, Justice ( who happens to be the Home
Secretary).”
 
24.4. The Department also informed the Committee that further advice has been solicited from the Ministry of Finance
on 19 December 2001, followed by reminders on 15 February and 21 March 2002 and the advice was awaited.
 
24.5     The Committee notes the observations of the Cabinet Secretariat in the matter. However, it finds it  difficult to
understand the advantages for the Government in keeping the anomaly intact. The Committee also does not agree with
the view of the Cabinet Secretariat that the Department of Justice is a full fledged separate Department headed by
Secretary, Justice who happens to be the Home Secretary. Rather the position, in the opinion of the Committee, is that
the Department of Justice is a full fledged separate Department headed by a Secretary who has to be the Home
Secretary. 
 
24.6     The Committee is of the considered view that the anomaly must be corrected and if need be the required change
in the Government  of India (Allocation of Business) Rules, 1961 may be effected so that the Department of Justice gets
a full fledged Secretary.

“TheCommittee is aware that for this state of affairs the Union Law Ministry is not blameworthy, as the entire
process of initiation of proposal for appointment of new judges is no longer the responsibility of the Executive as

question.  Against this backdrop the Committee recalls a recent discussion in the Rajya Sabha in which the
Government was asked regarding alternate arrangements to fill up the vacancies and whether there was any
scope for having a freshreview of the Supreme Court’s judgement.

However, the number of candidates belonging to these categories appointed as Notaries is  low even after a lapse of one
year since the Memorials were revised. The speed at which the applications are disposed of has also not improved. The
Government should, therefore, devise means to quicken the disposal at a faster pace and also launch a special drive to
fill the vacancies  in respect of the aforesaid categories.
 
5. National Legal Services Authority (NALSA)
 
 The Committee urges upon  the Government to operationalise  the accounting procedure of the National Legal Aid
Fund without further delay .  It  is also of the view that the Fund
should be utilised judiciously  so that,  needy people receive  legal aid. Further the Committee recommends to the
Government to provide funds for construction of  buildings for the Lok Adalats and the Legal Services Authorities at
various levelsso that they can carry out administration of justice smoothly.
 
 
6. Law Commission
 
The Committee feels that the Department of Legal Affairs should take up the work of overseeing the
implementation of  the Reports of Law Commission vigorously. The Committee is aware that the decisions regarding
implementation of a particular Report of the Law Commission is to be taken by the concerned administrative Ministry.
However, it is needless to say that the coordinating role of the Department is extremely important.
 
It is equally important that various recommendations contained in the Law Commission’s Reports should be
implemented expeditiously and that Parliament is apprised of the status of implementation of the recommendations.  In
this regard the Committee recommends to the Government to consider the introduction of the system of appending a
Memorandum of Action Taken to the Reports of the Law Commission at the time of laying the same in each House of
Parliament.
 
7. Legal Education
 
            The Committee had expressed its considered opinion in  the Seventy-second Report on Demands for Grants
(2001-2002) that the problems faced in the area of legal education  have to be looked at in-depth and there was
definitely a need for the Government to do a great deal more for improving the quality of legal education.  The
Committee would eagerly await the Report based on the study under taken by the  Law Commission and hopes that the
Government will urge upon the Commission to

expedite the study in order that the decline in standards and values in legal education are checked and the problems
being faced by the legal profession are obviated.
 
(ii) Legislative Department
 
 
8. Official Language Wing
 
A point was raised in the  Committee that the pocket edition of the Constitution was not easily available to the
common man.  In that contextthe Committee is happy to note that the Official Language Wing is planning to bring out
22,500 copies of the pocket edition of the Constitution in the current financial year. It would appreciate if the copies
were published in all Indian Languages and made available to the common man at an affordable price. 
 
The Committee is happy to note  that the authoritative text of the Constitution of India has already been brought
out in 15 regional languages and hopes that the Department would take expeditious action in respect of remaining
languages of the Eighth Schedule.
 
The Committee also desired that all the legislators in the country should be provided with a copy of  the
Constitution in the language of their choice included in the Eighth Schedule besides  copies in English and in the official
language. 
 
9. The Institute of Legislative Drafting and Research (ILDR)
 
The Committee is happy to note that the Department  proposes to  construct a separate building for the Institute
of Legislative Drafting and Research which is set to play an important role in training the officers of the Central,  State
and Union Territory Governments. The Committee has noted the progress so far viz, allotment of land and provision of
Rs. 1.55 crore in the Budget ( 2002-03) and hopes that the Institute becomes operational  from its new premises in the
shortest possible time,  as 4 to 5 years is a very long period. Meanwhile the Ministry should explore the possibility of
renting  suitable premises with required infrastructure  until the new premises are ready.
 
10. Electors’ Photo Identity Cards
 
The Committee takes a serious view of the tardy progress of   issue of  Electors’ Photo Identity Cards   to voters
in Bihar and Jharkhand and finds the explanation  given by the Government for not having any time limit for completion
of the programme of  issuing of photo identity cards to all the voters in the country, unacceptable. The Committee also
does not agree with the Ministry that issuing the photo identity cards is a programme  and not a  project and feels that 
this definitional escape reflects lack  of seriousness in completing the project in a given time frame.  Therefore, the
Committee urges the Government to take up the matter with the Election Commission so that Electors’ Photo Identity
Card are issued to all the electors in the country within a fixed time schedule.  
 
11. Electronic Voting Machines
 
The Committee notes the details of Electronic Voting Machines furnished by the Department and also the
explanation on the reliability aspect of these machines.  However, the Committee urges upon the Government to ensure
that EVMs are regularly monitored so as to promote greater public confidence in them.
 
 
(iii) Department Of Justice
 
12. Delinking of Budget of Department of Justice
 
The Committee notes the observations of the Cabinet Secretary in the matter. However, it finds it  difficult to
understand the advantages for the Government in keeping the anomaly intact. The Committee also does not agree with
the view of the Cabinet Secretary that the Department of Justice is a full fledged separate Department headed by

86th Report od Committee on Home Affair
file:///D/Committee%20on%20Home%20Affairs/86threport.htm[30-06-2016 17:49:15]
Secretary, Justice who happens to be the Home Secretary. Rather the position, in the opinion of the Committee, is that
the Department of Justice is a full fledged separate Department headed by a Secretary who has to be the Home
Secretary. 
 
The Committee is of the considered view that the anomaly must be corrected and if need be the required change
in the Government  of India (Allocation of Business) Rules, 1961 may be effected so that the Department of Justice gets
a full fledged Secretary.
 
13. Centrally Sponsored Scheme
 
The Committee is of the considered  view that the development of infrastructure  for Judiciary is key to smooth 
administration of Justice.  The Centrally Sponsored Scheme has been a good beginning in this direction.   However, the
funds provided under this scheme do not seem to be enough, particularly  looking at the projected demands of the States
which is more than 400 crore, whereas the Planning Commission has only earmarked Rs. 18 Crore in the B.E. 2002-
2003.
 
            The Committee in its 85
th Report (2001) on Law’s Delays:  Arears in Courts had pointed out  that the budget
allocation for judiciary is only 0.2 per cent of the GNP, out of which 50% i.e. 0.1  was  realised from the Court
revenues.  It is against  this  fact that the Committee feels, there is a strong case for increasing the budget allocation for
judiciary. This will also take care of the demands of the States already mentioned above.
 
            The Committee in its 72
nd Report (2001)  on Demands for Grants (2001-2002) had urged upon the Government
to consider enhancing the Central support to the State Governments.  The Committee while reiterating its previous
recommendation takes this opportunity to suggest to the Government to redesign the pattern of  Centre-State share so
that the States would have less budgetary pressure on them.
 
14. Construction of Lawyers Chambers and Litigant halls
 
The Committee is optimistic that the norms would be relaxed and permission granted so that construction of
lawyers chambers and halls for litigants/witnesses could be taken up by the Ministry on priority basis and a suitable
budgetary provision made for this.
 
15. Computerisation of City Civil Courts in Four Metropolitan Cities
 
The Committee entirely agrees with the Ministry that the judiciary is in dire need of modernisation and urges 
upon the Government to carry out the Scheme on a priority basis. 
 
16. Vacancies of Judges
 
            The Committee notes with serious concern the information furnished by the Department as mentioned in Para
27.6 Supra.
 
The  Committee having noted the replies of the Department of Justice, reiterates its
observations/recommendations made in its 85
th Report and calls upon the Government to take steps to restore the pre-
1993 position of appointment of Judges of the Supreme Court and High Courts.
 
17. All India Judicial Service
 
            The Committee feels that creation of the All India Judicial Service should be taken up more vigorously by the
Department. As per the reply, there are only two newly created State Governments and two High Courts which are yet
to send their comments.  Having come so close to a situation like this, the Committee strongly feels, that the
Government should expedite the matter within a given timeframe.

18. Family Courts
 
            The Committee notes that number of Family Courts in the States of Assam, Bihar, Jammu & Kashmir,
Uttaranchal, Orissa and West Bengal are markedly low whereas these States are  quite populous.  The Parliamentary
Committee on Empowerment of  Women during 2001-2002 has also pointed out that there are only 85 Family Courts in
the country although the Family Courts Act was enacted in 1984.  In this background the Committee is in agreement
with the Parliamentary Committee on Empowerment of Women’s recommendation for establishment of more family
courts not only in cities having one million population as provided in the Act,  but also in small cities having more than
1 lakh of population.  This will definitely reduce burden of the regular courts.
 
 
19. Pendency of Cases
 
The Committee takes serious view on the huge pendency of cases in High Courts and Subordinate Courts and
recommends that immediate steps be taken to reduce the pendency.  The Committee directs the Department of Justice to
give more emphasis on infrastructual development of High Courts and Subordinate Courts. 
 
Filling up of vacancies, creating more Family Courts and Fast Track Courts, Lok Adalats and Computerisation
which will go a long way in early disposal of cases.
 
20.Fast Track Courts
 
The Committee recommends that necessary steps be taken to make functional all the 1064 Fast Track Courts
which have been notified.
 
21. Judge-Population Ratio
 
            The Committee is happy to note that the Supreme Court has taken cognizance of the recommendations of this
Committee to increase  the Judge-population ratio and recommends that the Government may take necessary action for
providing additional funds for creation of infrastructural facilities for new judges to be added to the existing strength per
year.
 
22. Customary Law Courts
 
There are many tribal areas in our country especially in the North East where neither customary law  courts  nor judicial
courts exist. In district like Karbi Anglong of Assam, the executive magistrates  are trying all sorts of cases.  The
Committee observes that this practice  is against the basic tenets  of  jurisprudence.   It, therefore, recommends that the
Government should undertake a survey of such areas particularly in the north east  and wherever required either
customary law courts or judicial courts be established expediously. Regarding the financial requirements, the benefits of
the Centrally Sponsored Schemes should be extended for this purpose.
 
(iv) Department of Company Affairs
 
            
23. Company Law Board (CLB)
 
 
The Ministry in reply said that the Company Law Board is proposed to be replaced by National Company Law
Tribunal (NCLT) as proposed in the Companies (Amendment) Bill, 2001.  In view of this, no new members of the CLB
are being appointed.  As a result, the CLB has only three members against the sanctioned strength of nine members, and
as against four members available last year.  However, this concern is being brought to the notice of CLB.
 
The Committee feels that this is not a healthy state of  affair.  It disapproves the attitude of the Department in not
filling up the vacant posts of Members of CLB presupposing the creation of the National Company Law Tribunal.  The

Committee is of the view that all the vacancies in Company Law Board should be filled up and it be allowed to function
normally till it is replaced by a new law.
 
24. Investors’ Education and Protection Fund (IEPF)
 
The Committee notes the reply of the Department, however, it recommends that investor education should be
taken up in right earnest to protect the interest of investors
 
25. Inspection of Companies
 
 
 
The Committee feels that the inspection of companies who are not performing well or there are complaints
against whom be done irrespective of the number.   If the Department  does not have enough staff to carry out the
inspections, it should demand for more such staff because the Committee is of opinion that a constant monitoring of
companies is prerequisite to improving their health.  
 
26. Centre for Corporate Excellence
 
The Department informed that it has proposed to set up a centre for Corporate Excellence for better corporate
governance .  The proposed Centre for Corporate Excellence would have three broad functions: (i)  Research and
Studies (ii) Education, Promotion and Development  (iii) Accreditation and Awards with respect to matters bearing
upon corporate governance  and  excellence.  Its role would mainly be to serve as a knowledge portal and repository in
the field of corporate governance and excellence.
           
The Committee observed that new situation has developed all over the world as regards corporate governance is
concerned .  Good governance in the corporate world has become a key word .    Therefore, the Committee welcomes
the proposal to set up Centre for Excellence for Corporate Governance which is the need of the day.  However, 
Committee would appreciate a faster action on the part of the Government to make the Centre a reality.

            The management of personnel policies in Government of India, to begin with, was the joint responsibility of the Ministries of Home Affairs (Services and Establishment Wing) and Finance (Establishment Division) with Union Public Service Commission playing an important advisory
role. The Establishment Officer to the Government of India, functioning under the Cabinet Secretary had an important role to play in the senior appointments under the Government of India. All this made for improper division of responsibility and lack of a unified central direction.
 
2.         To plug this organisational loophole, the Estimates Committee of the Third Lok Sabha in its 93rd Report (April 1966) observed that “the ever expanding role of the government in a welfare state with its natural concomitant of a large civil service calls for effective personnel control
through a single agency”. The Administrative Reforms Commission too urged upon the Government to set up a separate Department of Personnel, to be placed directly under the Prime Minister to serve as a nodal agency for the personnel functions of the Government.
 
3.         The Union Government accepted this recommendation and as a consequence the ‘Department of Personnel’ was set up in August, 1970 and placed within the Cabinet Secretariat. In February, 1973, the Department of Administrative Reforms, till then with the Ministry of Home Affairs,
was amalgamated with the Department of Personnel and the newly created department was christened, the ‘Department of Personnel and Administrative Reforms’. In 1977, this department was transferred to the Ministry of Home Affairs. In March, 1985 a full fledged ‘Ministry of Personnel,
Public Grievances and Pensions’ was created.
 
4.0       The Ministry is the coordinating agency of the Central Government in personnel matters especially issues concerning recruitment, training, career development, staff welfare as well as the process of responsive people–oriented modern administration.  The Ministry comprises three
Departments, namely: -
 
(i)         Department of Personnel and Training;
(ii)        Department of Pensions and Pensioners’ Welfare; and
(iii)
               Department of Administrative Reforms and Public Grievances.
 
4.1       The Ministry has under its administrative control  four attached offices and four other offices, namely: -
 
            (i)         Central Bureau of Investigation (CBI);
(ii)
                Staff Selection Commission (SSC);
(iii)               Institute of Secretariat Training and Management (ISTM); and
(iv)              Lal Bahadur Shastri National Academy of Administration (LBSNAA).
 
4.1.1    The other offices under the administrative control of the Ministry are: -
 
(i)
                  Union Public Service Commission (UPSC), a constitutional body;
(ii)                Central Vigilance Commission (CVC), proposed to be converted into a statutory body;
(iii)               Central Administrative Tribunal (CAT), a statutory quasi-judicial body; and
(iv)              Public Enterprises Selection Board (PESB), a body set up by the resolution of Government.
 
5.         The Ministry is under the overall charge of the Prime Minister, assisted by a Minister of State.  All the three Departments are functioning under the charge of the Secretary (Personnel) assisted by one Special  Secretary, three Additional Secretaries and three Joint Secretaries and other
supporting officers and staff.
 
 
DEPARTMENT OF PERSONNEL AND TRAINING AND THE VARIOUS AGENCIES UNDER ITS ADMINISTRATIVE CONTROL
 
 
6.0       The role of the Department of Personnel and Training can be conceptually divided into two parts.  In its larger nodal role, it acts as the formulator of policy and the watch dog of the Government ensuring that certain accepted standards and norms, as laid down by it, are followed by all
Ministries/Departments in the recruitment, regulation of service conditions and deputation of personnel as well as other related issues.  Towards this end, guidelines are issued by it for the benefit of all Ministries/Departments and it monitors the implementation of these guidelines.  It also advises
all organisations of the Central Government  on issues of personnel management.  At a more immediate level, the Department has the direct responsibility of being the cadre controlling authority for the Indian Administrative Service (IAS) and the Central Secretariat Service (CSS).  The
Department also operates the Central Staffing Scheme under which suitable officers from  All India Services and Group ‘A’ Central Services are selected and then placed in posts at the level of Deputy Secretary, Director and Joint Secretary on the basis of tenure deputation.  The Department also
deals with cases of appointment to posts of Chairmen, Managing Directors, full-time functional Directors/Members of the Board of Management of various public sector undertakings/enterprises, corporations, banks and financial institutions.  It also deals with the assignment of Indian experts to
various developing countries.
 
Recruitment Agencies
6.1       The two organisations through which the Department ensures recruitment of personnel for the Government are the Union Public Service Commission (UPSC) and the Staff Selection Commission (SSC). The former is constituted under a provision of the Constitution and is responsible for
conducting examinations for appointment to the higher civil services and civil posts under the Union Government, including recruitment to the All India Services. There is a mandatory provision for consulting the Commission on all matters relating to methods of  recruitment, principles to be
followed in making promotions and transfers from one service to another and all the disciplinary matters. The SSC is responsible for making recruitment for Group ‘B’ non-gazetted posts of Assistants, Stenographers, etc.
 
Training Institutions
6.2       Two major training institutions directly under the administrative control of the Department are the Lal Bahadur Shastri National Academy of Administration (LBSNAA), Mussoorie and the Institute of Secretariat Training and Management (ISTM), New Delhi. The
former   is   mainly   responsible   for   providing   induction   training   to  recruits   to  the Indian Administrative Service and other All India Services and Central Services. The Institute of Training and Management provides induction as well as in-service training to members of
the Central Secretariat Service.
 
Senior Appointments under the Government of India
6.3       All proposals for senior appointments under the Government of India, which require the approval of the Appointments Committee of the Cabinet (ACC) under the Government of India (Transaction of Business) Rules, 1961are processed through the Establishment Officer as Secretary to
the ACC.  These include board level appointments to Central Public Sector Undertakings and appointments of Joint Secretaries, Directors and Deputy Secretaries in the Ministries/Departments. In addition, all appointments by promotion, which require the approval of the ACC are also processed
through the Establishment Officer.
 
 
Public Enterprises Selection Board (PESB)
 
6.4       The Public Enterprises Selection Board (PESB) is entrusted with the responsibility of making recommendations for appointment to the full-time Board level posts of Chief Executives and functional Directors and part-time Chairmen in the Central Public Undertakings.
 
 
Administrative Vigilance
 
6.5       The Department of Personnel and Training determines Government policy for the maintenance of integrity of the public services and eradication of corruption and coordinates the activities of various Ministries/Departments in that area.
 
Central Vigilance Commission (CVC)
6.6       Advice on all vigilance matters is provided by the Central Vigilance Commission. It has jurisdiction and power in respect of all matters to which the executive power of the Union Government extends. The Commission is also entrusted with the supervision of the Central Bureau of
Investigation (CBI). The Commission enjoys the same measure of independence and autonomy as the Union Public Service Commission.
 
 
Central Bureau of Investigation (CBI)
 
6.7       The Central Bureau of Investigation is the premier investigating agency of the country to investigate complex and important cases particularly relating to internal security, espionage, sabotage, narcotics, economic offences, cybercrimes and cases  registered under

87th Report of Committee on Home Affairs
file:///D/Committee%20on%20Home%20Affairs/87threport.htm[30-06-2016 17:50:17]
Prevention   of Corruption  Act.
 
Joint Consultative Machinery
6.8       The Joint Consultative Machinery (JCM) is three-tier machinery consisting of the National Council, the Departmental Council and the Regional/Office Council. Service matters pertaining to the interests of the generality of employees or specific groups of them are dealt
with by this machinery.
 
Central Administrative Tribunal (CAT)
6.9       In order to provide speedy and inexpensive justice to employees aggrieved by Government decisions, the Government has set up the Central Administrative Tribunal  (CAT) in 1985, which now dealswith all cases relating to service matters which were previously dealt with by Courts upto
and including the High Courts. 
 
 
Staff Welfare
 
6.10     The Department supports various programmes, which are provided in various Ministries/Departments, Central Government Employees Welfare Coordination Committee in Central Government offices located outside Delhi, Residents’ Welfare Associations/Area Welfare
Officers; Benevolent Fund and Departmental Canteens.  Department of Personnel and Training is the nodal agency for three registered societies set up  for the welfare of the Government employees and their families.  These societies are the Central Civil Services Cultural and
Sports Board, Grih Kalyan Kendra and Kendriya Bhandar. 
 
DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND PENSIONERS’ WELFARE
7.         The Department of Pension and Pensioners’ Welfare is the nodal agency of the Government of India for formulation of general policy on pension and other retirement benefits, as also for redressal of grievances on retirement benefits.  The Department was set up in 1985
as a part of Ministry of Personnel, Public Grievances and Pensions and has been rendering service for the benefit of pensioners since then.  The Department has taken a number of steps over the years for streamlining the pension administration system, for greater convenience
and welfare of the pensioners.
DEPARTMENT OF ADMINISTRATIVE REFORMS AND PUBLIC GRIEVANCES
8.         The Department of Administrative Reforms and Public Grievances is the nodal agency of the Government of India for administrative reforms as well as redressal of public grievances relating to the State in general and grievances pertaining to  Central Government agencies in particular.
The Department disseminates information on important activities of the Government relating to administrative reforms and public grievance redressal through Management Publications and Documentation.  This Department also acts as the nodal agency in regard to Organisation and Methods
activities and offers advice to the Ministries/Departments. It also undertakes activities in the field of international co-operation and exchanges to promote public service reforms.
CHAPTER-II

10.7.    The trend of decrease in the projection of Demands of the Ministry for the year 2002-2003 is perceivable in both Plan and Non-plan outlays.
 
Non-Plan outlay/Expenditure
 
10.8.0.The Non-plan budget of the Ministry has slightly decreased from Rs 179.61 crore in BE (2001-2002) to Rs 178.69 crore in BE (2002-2003) showing a sum of Rs 92 lakh reduction (i.e. 0.5 percent).  The Ministry in its explanatory note has stated that out of the Non-plan budget provision of
Rs 178.69 crore, Rs 90.23 crore (i.e. 50.49 % of the Non-plan budget) is for the Central Bureau of Investigation alone. Five percent of the Non-plan budget i.e. 8 crore is towards making payment of House Building Advance to All India Service Officers.  The remaining portions of the Budget
(45.03%) is meant for meeting the expenditure on administrative expenditure in respect of organizations and schemes mentioned at para 10.0 of the Report.
 
10.8.1.It may be observed from the analysis of BE and RE (2001-2002) that perceptible reduction has been effected for the provisions for Secretariat General Services (Ministry proper) and the CBI under Non-plan outlay.  The Ministry has stated in their explanatory note that the reduction is due
to the implementation of guidelines issued by Ministry of Finance for mandatory 10 per cent cut in the budgetary allocation for Non-plan and Non-salary expenditures.  The guidelines as outlined in the OM No.7(4)/E-Coord/2000 dated 24 September, 2000 of the Ministry of Finance are as
follows:-

87th Report of Committee on Home Affairs
file:///D/Committee%20on%20Home%20Affairs/87threport.htm[30-06-2016 17:50:17]
 
(i)                  There shall be a mandatory 10% cut in the Budgetary allocation for non-plan, non-salary expenditure of all Ministries/Departments and Autonomous Institutions.
(ii)                Utmost economy should be exercised in use of staff cars and official vehicles.  There shall be a 10% cut in the consumption and allocation of funds for expenditure on POL for staff cars.
(iii)               There will be a complete ban on purchase of new vehicles for one year.
(iv)              Implementation of existing instructions concerning 10% cut in posts and abolition of posts lying vacant for more than one year should be ensured.  There shall be a ban on creation on new posts in all Ministries/Departments/Autonomous institutions for one year.
(v)                Foreign travel should be restricted to unavoidable official engagements and there shall be a ban on foreign travel for Study Tours, Seminars etc.  Size of official delegations, where Foreign Travel is unavoidable, shall be restricted to the bare minimum.
(vi)              The permissible per diem allowance for travel abroad shall stand reduced by 25% for all countries and for all categories, officials/non officials.  These instructions shall also apply to autonomous institutions and PSUs. 
(vii)             Austerity should be reflected in organizing Conferences/Seminars/Workshops. Existing guidelines for holding such events and expenditure ceilings thereon should be enforced.
 
10.8.2.Keeping in view the above guidelines, the budget under Non-plan outlay at RE stage of 2001-2002 was reduced to Rs 174.08 crore (the provisional actual given in the explanatory note being the same) from Rs 179.61 crore (a net reduction of Rs 5.53 crores), which is approximately three
percent and is far behind the ten percent cut stipulated by the Ministry of Finance.  A comparison between BE (2001-2002) and BE (2002-2003) under the Non-plan outlay shows the decrease of a meagre amount of Rs 0.92 crore.  (0.5 percent)
 
10.8.3.While examining the Demands for Grants (2001-2002) of the Ministry, the Committee has enquired whether 10 percent job cut, as announced by the Finance Minister in his budget speech in 2001, during the next five years had been reflected in the BE (2001-2002).  The Ministry in its
reply had intimated that since the provision had been made before the announcement of budget speech, the proposed curtailment of posts had not been reflected in BE for the year 2001-2002 and would be reflected in RE stage of the same year.
 
10.8.4.A glance over the minor heads –Salaries of all three Departments of the Ministry under the Major Head  “2052”- Secretariat- General Services at BE & RE (2001-2002) and BE (2002-2003) lends credence to the reply given by the Ministry.  The minor head Salaries of the Central Bureau
of Investigation under the Major Head “2055”- Police does not show the tendency commensurating this reflection in other Departments of the Ministry as the BE & RE (2001-2002) for Salaries of the CBI being the same (Rs 61.7 crore). Further a glance over office expenses of Departments of the
Ministry shows no hike in BE (2002-03) from RE (2001-2002) except Department of Pensions and Pensioner’s Welfare.  The minor increase of Rs 50 thousand, in the office expenses of the Department of Pensions & Pensioner’s Welfare, as explained by the Ministry, is intended to cover office
requirements of this Department consequent upon some renovation work already taken.  The Committee has taken note of the curtailments in the heads narrated above.
 
10.8.5.The projection under the Minor Heads –Salaries of all Departments and attached bodies under Demand No. 63 is Rs 105.5130 crore in BE (2002-2003) as compared to Rs 102.48 crore in BE (2001-2002).  The provision for non-salary expenditure after excluding expenditure on Salaries
comes to Rs 108.177 crore and Rs 122.13 crore in BE (2002-2003) & BE (2001-2002), respectively. The variation of (-) Rs 13.953 crore between BE (2002-2003) and BE (2001-2002) for non-salary expenditure/projection forms (-) 11 percent which conforms to the guidelines of the Ministry of
Finance enumerated in its OM No.7 (4)/E-Coord/2000 dated 24 September 2000.  But it is not understood, from the variation of total Non-plan outlay between BE  (2001-2002) & BE (2002-2003), whether the Ministry has followed the guidelines of the M/o Finance while projecting BE (2002-
2003) under Non-plan outlay.  The 0.5 percent (i.e. Rs. 92 lakh only) reduction under Non-plan outlay of BE (2002-2003) is far behind the goal set by the M/o Finance. The Committee, therefore, desires that the Ministry of Personnel, Public Grievances and Pensions should strive to take austerity
measures to project more reduction at RE stage (2002-2003) to give effect to guidelines of the Ministry of Finance.

10.8.9  On being asked to furnish the salient features of Center for Public Policy Project and Policy on domestic funding of foreign training and components of outlay thereon, the Ministry has submitted the following:-
 
“The Government of India is setting up a Centre for Public Policy (CPP) at the Indian Institute of Management, Bangalore (IIMB) with a view to internalize some of the prestigious foreign programs on public policy and provide high quality academic programs for serving officers.  The
Centre is being funded partly through budgetary support (Rs. 8.82 crore) for creation of infrastructure and partly through UNDP grant assistance (US $ 2.16 million) to cover training fees for 75 officers, faculty development, expansion of computer center, strengthening of library,
development of modules, foreign collaboration, etc.
 
            A scheme for the domestic funding of foreign training has been introduced because external support, which was earlier available for foreign training of serving officers, has been almost entirely withdrawn by the funding agencies.  Continuance of foreign training has been considered
essential since Indian development plans have to take into account the emerging international scenario. The proposed Scheme comprises three components, namely:-
 
(a)                Long term training of officers under which about 25-30 officers would be deputed every year;

DEMAND NO.-96 (UNION PUBLIC SERVICE COMMISSION)
 
11.0     The Union Public Service Commission is a constitutional body, created under Article 315 of the Constitution.  The Commission’s charter of duties is given in Articles 320 and 321 of the Constitution.  In brief, it is the duty of the Commission to conduct examinations for appointment to
services of the Union and to advise Government on all matter relating to framing of recruitment rules, method of recruitment and the principle to be followed in making promotions and transfers from one service to another.  The Commission is also required to be consulted in respect of
disciplinary matters affecting a civil servant including appeals and memoranda filed by individual Government servants.  The Commission’s advice is also sought regarding any claim for reimbursement of legal proceedings instituted against him for acts done in execution of his duties and on the
question of award of pension for injury sustained by a Government servant in a civil capacity.  By virtue of the provisions made in the relevant Acts, the Commission is required to be consulted in respect of appointments to certain categories of posts under the Municipal Corporation of Delhi, the
Employees’ State Insurance Corporation and the Employees’ Provident Fund Organization.
 
11.1     Article 322 of the Constitution envisages inter-alia that the expenses of the UPSC including salaries, allowances and pensions payable to members and staff of the Commission shall be ‘charged’ on the Consolidated Fund of India.  A statement indicating the BE and RE (2001-2002) and
